title: Control-plane segmentation for hybrid hosting proposal
content:
Summary:

This note captures a lightweight proposal and trade study for introducing a segmented control plane model to support hybrid hosting across Hosted API, Dedicated capacity, and Private (VPC/on-prem) deployments for POC customers. The idea: keep control-plane responsibilities we do well in Redwood-hosted services (billing, orchestration, model catalog, telemetry ingestion endpoint) while allowing the inference data path and critical tenant-specific control surface to run inside customer-controlled infrastructure when requested. Goal is to balance operational speed, data sovereignty, and predictable economics for POCs while minimizing integration friction.

Context and motivation:
- Recent POC requests from regulated customers want low-latency inference + auditable model execution within their VPC but still want Redwood to manage model lifecycle and rollouts.
- Full private deployments take too long (network setup, certs, access reviews). Pure-hosted keeps time-to-value but fails data isolation or egress constraints.
- We need an intermediate, low-friction option for 4-12 week POCs that reduces risk and accelerates validation.

Proposed conceptual model ("segmented control plane"):
1) Control plane (hosted by Redwood): user/tenant metadata, model catalog entries, rollout policies, billing, management API, and non-sensitive aggregated telemetry.
2) Tenant-local runtime components (in customer VPC or Dedicated subnet): inference workers, KV cache, request ingress endpoint, and a small "control agent" that receives signed, minimal routing/rollout decisions from the hosted control plane.
3) Secure sync channel: mTLS tunnels initiated by tenant-local agent to Redwood control plane for policy updates, model artifact pulls (optionally via signed blob storage), and health/metrics push.
4) Data flow: application -> tenant ingress (customer VPC) -> local inference worker -> (optional) prefix cache; artifacts and model binaries pulled securely; enterprise logs and raw data do not transit Redwood-hosted network unless explicitly allowed.

Design alternatives considered (short):
- Option 1: Fully hosted (status quo)
  - Pros: fastest onboarding, simplest ops, unified telemetry.
  - Cons: fails for customers with data sovereignty/egress constraints; potential latency for regional customers.

- Option 2: Segmented control plane (proposed)
  - Pros: preserves Redwood management controls, reduces onboarding time vs full private, satisfies many sovereignty/latency constraints, easier rollback/fallback to hosted models.
  - Cons: introduces a new security boundary, requires small customer network & IAM work, needs hardened agent and upgrade path.

- Option 3: Full private control plane + runtime (customer-managed control plane)
  - Pros: maximal isolation & compliance, customer fully in control.
  - Cons: longest lead time, more expensive for both sides, replicates operational complexity.

Key technical tradeoffs and decisions to make:
- Model binary distribution: signed blobs from Redwood S3-like store vs. customer pulls from mirrored registries. Trade: security and trust vs. bandwidth/latency.
- Rollout policy enforcement: remote decisions pushed to agent vs. agent polling for delta. Trade: complexity vs. offline resilience.
- KV/prefix cache placement: local only vs. shared cache with optional snapshot uploads. Trade: cost per token vs. reproducibility.
- Fallback behavior: automatic overflow to hosted inference when local pool saturated vs. hard reject. Trade: availability vs. data egress.

Operational concerns and mitigations:
- Upgrades: agent must support zero-downtime upgrades and graceful fallback to hosted routing rules if incompatible. Plan: semantic version check and conservative rolling updates in agent manifest.
- Auditing: include request-level hashes and signed trace headers so hosted control plane can reconstruct events without receiving raw prompts.
- Key management: integrate with customer KMS for encryption of local model artifacts and optionally with Redwood KMS for signatures.
- SLA and billing: separate metering for local inference (reported by agent) and hosted control plane operations. Ensure usage reconciliation flow in case of drift.
- Security review: provide an explicit threat model doc and hardened agent; require customer network ACL checklist before POC starts.

Preliminary cost/latency estimates (POC scale, modeled for 2-4 GPU pod local):
- Setup effort: ~5-10 engineer-hours coordination + 1 solutions engineer onsite/remote session.
- Infra cost delta vs hosted: +20-40% due to reserved capacity and egress (depends on model size).
- Median p50 latency reduction: 10-35% for colocated VPCs (depends on region).

Risk register (top items):
- Agent compromise or misconfiguration -> potential control-plane spoofing. Mitigation: signing, attestation, regular scans, allowlisted IPs.
- Metrics reconciliation gaps -> billing disputes. Mitigation: checksum-based metering + nightly reconciliation job and audit log retention.
- Slow artifact distribution -> cold-start microbursts. Mitigation: pre-warm options and delta-only model patching.

Operational runbook sketch (POC):
- Pre-POC checklist: network ACLs, KMS key ready, agent container image whitelist, contact points. (Owner: SE)
- Day 0: provision local VPC subnet + small GPU pool (1-2 GPUs), install agent, validate mTLS handshake (Owner: Customer infra)
- Day 1-3: push model artifacts, run synthetic latency and correctness tests, validate logs (Owner: SE + Eng)
- Week 1-2: run live traffic shadowing, monitor quality metrics, iterate prompts/quantization profile (Owner: Customer PM + SE)
- Rollback plan: disable control-plane policy push and route traffic to hosted model pool; preserve local artifacts for forensics.

Open engineering questions (notes to self):
- Should agent support sidecar pattern vs standalone VPC appliance? Sidecar easier for k8s customers, appliance simpler for on-prem. Need both?
- How to signal to Hosted API that a particular request must never leave the VPC even for fallback? Proposal: request-level policy header, validated by agent with customer-signed token.
- Data retention spec for telemetry: store only top-level counts in hosted plane, raw events in customer log forwarder by default.

Action items and next steps:
- Build small spike repo showing agent handshake + model pull (ENG-4321) (Owner: Infra Eng, due 2025-02-14)
- Draft threat model and run internal security review with SecOps (Owner: Security, due 2025-02-21)
- Create SE POC checklist doc and template for customer onboarding (Owner: Solutions Eng, due 2025-02-07)
- Pricing sketch for POC and for 12-month reserved hybrid offering (Owner: FinOps + Product, due 2025-02-28)

Appendix: terse example flow for fail-open vs fail-closed policy
- Fail-open (preferred for availability): local agent checks capacity; if overloaded, it returns a signed overflow token to control plane; control plane attempts to route to hosted pool when customer policy allows.
- Fail-closed (preferred for strict sovereignty): local agent rejects requests when capacity insufficient. Customer must opt in.

Quick list of docs to author after this note (short):
- Agent security & attestation spec
- Model artifact distribution protocol (signed deltas)
- SE POC runbook template
- Pricing + SLA delta memo

Notes-to-self: get time on calendar with Priya and Marta to validate KMS options; call with AcmeHealth infra team next week to gauge appetite for fail-open fallback.

End of note.
